topic: How mutable and immutable variables work in Python
learn: Why b = a is a second name, not a copy
Which Python types change in place and which are replaced
How the mutable default argument bug gets written

title.main: In Python, a name is a sticker, not a box
title.sub: Two names can sit on one object. Whether it can change is what makes lists and strings behave differently.

stages.title: You changed b, a changed too
stages.desc: A list assigned to a second name is not a copy. Both names sit on one object.

stages.title: b = a copies the sticker
stages.desc: The list is built once in memory. The second line just points another name at it.

stages.title: A list is mutable
stages.desc: append edits the object itself. The id never changes, so both names show the new value.

stages.title: A string is immutable
stages.desc: It cannot be edited, so += builds a new object and moves only that one name.

stages.title: Which types are which
stages.desc: Numbers, strings and tuples cannot change. Lists, dicts and sets can.

stages.title: This is the classic bug
stages.desc: A mutable default argument is created once, then quietly reused by every call.

stages.title: The fix is a fresh object
stages.desc: Default to None and build the list inside, or copy before you mutate.

stages.title: Mutate or rebind
stages.desc: Every confusing line in Python comes down to which of these two it is doing.

end.title: Names point. Objects change, or they do not.
end.sub: Mutable objects change in place and every name sees it. Immutable objects are replaced, and only one name moves.

post.caption:
b = a does not copy your list.

Both names point at the same object, so b.append(4) changes what a shows. A string does the opposite — s += "!" cannot edit the string, so Python builds a new one and moves only s.

That single idea explains the mutable default argument bug too.

Which one caught you first?
